item.title: Man jailed for murder after denying son, 14, treatment for Covid
item.description:
Man jailed for murder after denying son, 14, treatment for Covid

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A Dutch man whose 14-year-old son died after he was denied medical treatment for Covid-19 has been jailed for 23 years by a court in Belgium.

Rennlhy Manuela covered up the death of his son, Jairon, for eight weeks, refusing to let his siblings enter his bedroom and telling his mother he was out of the house when she tried to visit him.

Manuela, who belonged to a strict Pentecostal sect, refused to consult a doctor when Jairon fell ill at the end of 2021, instead relying on paracetamol, a liquid diet and prayers for his recovery.

The court of justice in Antwerp said Manuela “made his child’s life subordinate to his radical religious convictions”. He was convicted of murder by a jury and sentenced to 23 years in prison, three years more than prosecutors demanded.

The boy died in the night of January 3 and 4 after falling in the bath. When police were called to the house, they found his body underneath a blanket in an advanced state of decay, with traces of ketamine in his blood.

Manuela and his adult housemates had hoped God would answer their prayers to bring Jairon back to life.

Mother raised alarm

Jairon’s mother, Danica, raised the alarm after she contacted the boy’s school across the Dutch border in Tilburg, only to be told he had been signed out months earlier.

She had been denied access to the villa in Turnhout, where Manuela lived with his children and several other members of the religious community.

Four other adults were given sentences of between one and three years in the case. The jury said Manuela had caused “irreperable suffering” by “preventing [Jairon’s] mother and brothers saying goodbye in a humane manner”.

item.title: One-third of drinking water supplies contain high levels of PFAS
item.description:
One-third of drinking water supplies contain high levels of PFAS

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Water companies have called for PFAS chemicals to be banned in pesticides after a study showed that one-third of people are exposed to high levels of the “forever chemicals” in drinking water.

An analysis by Greenpeace of every postcode in the Netherlands showed that the water in 32% of areas contains PFAS levels that are at least 1.5 times the recommended safe level.

The environmental inspection agency ILT blames the increased use of trifluoroacetic acid in pesticides by agricultural sectors such as potato farming, which has almost doubled in the last two years. The ILT says two tonnes of the chemical end up in the water supply per year.

The highest concentrations are in the provinces of Noord-Holland, Zuid-Holland and Zeeland, with towns such as Zaandam, Purmerend and IJmuiden recording 14.3 nanograms per litre.

PFAS is a collective label for thousands of highly stable chemical compounds that are used extensively in packaging, liquid chemicals and products such as waterproof clothing and non-stick cooking pans.

They are attractive to industry because they are extremely durable, but prolonged exposure increases the risk of cancer, immune system problems, low fertility and damage to unborn babies.

High blood levels

A recent study by the public health agency RIVM showed almost everyone in the Netherlands has unhealthy levels of PFAS in their blood.

Greenpeace compiled a dataset and built an online tool allowing householders to see how much PFAS is in their drinking water, with a map to show the most polluted and least polluted areas.

“We think this information should be available to everyone, so we asked a data analyst to set out clearly how much pollution is in the water per location,” campaign leader Eline Bosman told NRC.

There are strong regional variations, with the northern provinces of Drenthe, Friesland and Groningen showing almost no PFAS chemicals in drinking water.

Patricia van der Linden of Vewin, the association of Dutch drinking water suppliers, said the west of the country drew its water supply from rivers and reservoirs, which are more polluted than water sources in rural areas.

“Ground water contains less pollution than surface water,” she said. “In places where we use surface water for drinking water, we have to take more steps to purify the water.”

Immune system

Although none of the water supplies exceed the legal limit set by the European Union, they are well above the RIVM’s advisory limit of 4.4 nanograms.

The agency lowered the guideline level in 2023 in the light of new information that showed PFAS chemicals have a greater impact on the immune system than previously thought.

Germany, the Netherlands and the Scandinavian nations have been lobbying since February 2023 for a total ban on PFAS in pesticides throughout the EU.

RIVM spokesman Coen Berends told NRC: “We can see that banning individual types of PFAS makes a difference, but really the whole group should be banned.”

item.title: Student who made Hitler salute at TU Eindhoven has left NL
item.description:
Student who made Hitler salute at TU Eindhoven has left NL

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The public prosecution service has said it will not investigate an incident involving a Hitler salute during a lecture at TU Eindhoven after the student voluntarily left the country.

According to the university, a during a first year calculus class, the student made racist remarks in the packed lecture hall and performed a Nazi salute. Fellow students intervened, resulting in a fight.

The university executive board said in a statement that the behaviour was “unacceptable” and it was investigating.

The student was later arrested on suspicion of threatening behaviour, but prosecutors dropped the case because he was deemed to be “vulnerable”.

Following talks with the student and his father, the youth, who turned 18 this month, choose to leave the Netherlands, the public prosecution service said. They would not disclose his country of origin.

item.title: Ahead of Jetten’s UN address, worries about ICC sanctions
item.description:
Ahead of Jetten’s UN address, worries about ICC sanctions

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

As prime minister Rob Jetten heads to New York to address the United Nations General Assembly, multiple news outlets have reported that the Trump administration is set to sanction the International Criminal Court (ICC).

The Wall Street Journal, Reuters and the Associated Press have all reported in recent days that the United States is planning to escalate its fight with the ICC and sanction the institution as a whole.

The White House has already sanctioned 13 staff members, including the court’s president, Japanese Judge Tomoko Akane, over the investigation into allegedly Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

In 2024, the court issued arrest warrants for Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other for war crimes.

Foreign affairs minister Tom Berendsen is also traveling to New York for the UN’s annual meeting. According to his agenda, he is set to meet with other world leaders to discuss the ICC, as well as the situation in Ukraine.

Earlier this year, Berendsen said in a statement that the Netherlands “disapproves” of the sanctions against ICC staff.

Host state

Jetten’s public schedule does not including any specific meetings about the ICC. He will address the UN on Thursday.

As the court’s host state, the Dutch are obligated to provide assistance such as cooperation with security, facilitating visas and helping with transportation for defendants and witnesses.

A number of opposition parties in the Netherlands feel the government is not doing enough to protect the institution. MP Kati Piri of Pro told public broadcaster NOS that the cabinet has adopted a “super weak” stance so far.

In a letter to parliament earlier this month, Berendsen said the Dutch had been regularly meeting with the court and other countries to discuss the situation, writing that “Dutch efforts have contributed to the Court’s ability … to continue the vast majority of its operations unimpeded thus far.”

item.title: Attacks on fire stations increase as gangs target hydraulic gear
item.description:
Attacks on fire stations increase as gangs target hydraulic gear

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Fire stations are struggling with a wave of break-ins as criminal gangs target hydraulic equipment that can be used to smash cashpoints and roller shutters.

In the last month alone police have recorded 25 attacks on fire stations, compared to 35 in the two years 2024 and 2025, according to figures shared with TV real crime show Opsporing Verzocht.

So far this year there have been 85 break-ins, most recently on Monday night at Maarn-Maarsbergen in Utrecht province. Police said hydraulic tools such as spreaders were increasingly being found at the scene of ram-raids on retailers such as such as jewellers and electronics stores.

“A hydraulic spreader, for example, is intended for things like freeing people from car wrecks, but now they’re being used to destroy roller shutters and cash machines,” a spokesman said.

The thefts are also leaving fire stations short of vital equipment needed to save lives. But managers are reluctant to take extra safety measures such as locking tools away because it takes longer to retrieve them in an emergency, when every second counts.

The service told NOS it was considering stepping up less intrusive measures such as installing CCTV cameras and reflective glass to hide the contents of fire stations.

item.title: Government draws up 50-point plan to speed up housebuilding
item.description:
Government draws up 50-point plan to speed up housebuilding

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan has drawn up details of a 50-point plan to speed up housebuilding to meet the target of 100,000 new homes a year.

The previous government identified 26 sites near railway stations that are already well served by transport links and utilities, making them relatively easy to develop.

Another five locations were pinpointed in Maastricht, Haarlem, Leeuwarden, Deventer and Weert, earlier this year, with more five due to be announced by the end of 2026. All 10 developments are supposed to be finished by 2040.

The cabinet is investing €7 billion over the next eight years in affordable homes and wants to scrap planning rules and building requirements that slow down the process.

Affordable homes are supposed to account for two-thirds of all new projects, with at least 30% going on social housing.

Around €3 billion of the funding will take the form of subsidies, while investors who build houses for the mid-rental sector will receive a payment for each unit they construct from 2029.

The government is anxious to retain private investors who have been selling rental flats in response to the Affordable Rent Act, which has tightened the rules used to calculate rent levels, and lingering uncertainty over the “box 3” tax on income from assets.

Local and regional subsidies

Local councils will be encouraged to buy land for housing, with the national government providing financial support to share the risk. The municipalities and provinces will also be able to hire 200 equivalent full-time staff to work on issuing permits, while a team of experts will tour the country using their specialist knowledge to revive projects that have become stuck in the system.

Analysts noted that some of the regulations would have the effect of pumping more money into existing plans. “That means that some building projects probably won’t go ahead because they’re not profitable,” Stefan Groot, housing market economist for Rabobank, told NRC.

Boekholt-O’Sullivan said: “I will continue with what works and reform what doesn’t. It is clear what has to happen, money is avaiable and there are enough building projects.

“What matters now is moving from the drawing board to the foundations. The government can’t do it alone: we need builders, investors, local authorities and provinces to work with us.”

* This article has been corrected. An earlier version said the government had identified 50 sites for housebuilding.

item.title: Heineken set to buy pub portfolio from debt-laden UK landlord
item.description:
Heineken set to buy pub portfolio from debt-laden UK landlord

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam-based brewing giant Heineken is poised to buy 300 pubs from Britain’s largest pub owner, Stonegate, in a €350 million deal.

Heineken is reported to have been holding talks over the summer with Stonegate, which is seeking to reduce its debts of £3 billion (€3.5 billion) by selling 1,000 of its 4,500 outlets.

Most of the debt is related to the British company’s decision to purchase Enterprise Inns in 2019, just before the coronavirus pandemic shut down the entire British pub sector for several months.

Pubs have also been struggling with the rapidly rising cost of beer, energy, wages and higher taxes on employers.

Heineken already owns around 2,350 pubs in Britain through its subsidiary Star Pubs & Bars.

item.title: Council of State: freeze “disproportionate” traffic fines
item.description:
Council of State: freeze “disproportionate” traffic fines

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Council of State has urged the cabinet to rethink its decision to raise traffic fines amid concerns that the penalties have increased out of proportion to other offences.

Justice minister David van Weel wants to raise fines across the board by 2.7% next year, in line with inflation.

If approved, the new fines would include €130 for parking without authorisation, €330 for running red lights and €450 for using a mobile phone at the wheel.

Speeding fines depend on the actual speed, ranging from €33 for going 4km/h over the limit to €424 for exceeding the limit by 30km/h. But fines are higher in built-up areas and 30km zones: driving 50km/h in a 30km/h limit will cost €351.

The Council of State, which issues non-binding advice on all government bills and decisions, queried if the raise was “necessary, fair and proportionate”, echoing criticism from other legal bodies in recent years.

They include the prosecution service (Openbare Ministerie), judges and the agency that collects the fines, the CJI, which said there was “imbalance” with fines for other offences such as common assault, which typically carries a penalty of €400.

Debt problems

Traffic fines have increased cumulatively by 220% in the last 30 years, while in 2024 127,000 families had problems with debt caused by outstanding traffic penalties.

The Council of State said freezing the fines rather than allowing them to rise with inflation was a “first obvious step” towards rebalancing the penalties.

It said the reason given by ministers – that the income from fines was needed to meet the justice ministry’s costs – was not a valid legal argument.

“The aim of these fines is to sanction behaviour that breaks the rules and improve road safety,” it said in a written advisory. “Raising the tariffs for traffic fines should relate to serving that purpose.”

item.title: Urgent help needed for children in emergency asylum shelters
item.description:
Urgent help needed for children in emergency asylum shelters

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Children in emergency shelters are living in unsafe and dangerous conditions that violate international law, according to a two-year investigation by the Dutch Safety Board.

The organisation has been looking into the living situation for some 7,000 children who are currently living in crisis accommodations while awaiting the outcome of their asylum claims.

Children experience constant noise and a total lack of privacy in these shelters as well as a high risk of physical and sexual violence, the report found.

The safety board wants the immigration ministry to make sweeping reforms in the next six months.

“Emergency shelter is not normal. It was initially intended for a short period, but by now, children sometimes live in emergency shelters for years,” the organisation’s chairperson Chris van Dam said in a statement.

More than 60% of asylum seekers are now being housed in “emergency” shelters, like vacant offices, ships, event halls, and temporary container homes.

The safety board wants a structural solution to the shelter problems as well as improvements in emergency shelters, including setting a maximum length of stay and enforcing quality standards.

item.title: Maastricht and son of André Rieu at odds over Christmas decor
item.description:
Maastricht and son of André Rieu at odds over Christmas decor

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Maastricht has limited how Pierre Rieu can decorate his hotel in the Limburg capital, telling the son of famous musician André Rieu that his current proposal is too extravagant.

Rieu had proposed to turn the historic city centre building into a life-sized Christmas gift, with string lights and an illuminated bow.

The 4-star Hotel Derlon dates from 1870 and was bought by Rieu in 2025.

He had done up the hotel in the same manner last year, but the city’s Planning and Monuments Commission found the decorations to be excessive, according to local news outlet L1.

The hotelier was told he needed to choose between the bow and the string lights to allow the building’s architecture to be visible.

Rieu told regional broadcaster 1Zuid he was irritated with the decision. “We’re talking about Christmas lights. I don’t think anyone is bothered by that,” he said.
